strategy_summary.headline: There is no shared database to decompose. The real decomposition work for this application is INTRA-ASSEMBLY design debt, not data-tier disentanglement, and it is owned by the code-structure line rather than by this skill.
strategy_summary.where_the_actual_work_lives: The structural analysis identified three intra-module boundaries and one explicit non-boundary: extract the item rules plus the domain model out of the entry-point class into a referencable library (cut first; it unblocks the others); leave composition, seed-data acquisition and invocation behind as a host concern; re-point the orphaned test assembly at the extracted library with characterisation tests before any refactor; and explicitly NO service decomposition is warranted at 172 lines, one deployable, zero endpoints, zero integrations and zero tables.

co_wave_constraints.basis: An application with no database cannot be entangled with any other application through shared data, so it constrains nobody and is constrained by nobody on data grounds. An empty constraint set is a meaningful result here, not a missing analysis.

write_ownership_after_cutover.basis: Write ownership is vacuous: there are no tables, therefore no shared table has contested or ambiguous write ownership, and no dual-write arrangement is proposed or needed. The singular-write-ownership rule is satisfied trivially.
write_ownership_after_cutover.in_process_state_note: The application's only mutable state is an in-memory item list owned exclusively by the single console process for the duration of one run. The documented invariants (quality never negative, never above 50, Sulfuras pinned at 80) are enforced nowhere but as conditionals inside that one loop, and the domain model exposes unguarded public setters — so the invariants are code-level, not data-level, constraints. If a persistent store is ever introduced they must be re-established as data constraints.

If this application record denotes a production system whose inventory persists in a store owned by another application, that store is invisible to a static walk and this strategy would be resolving a decomposition problem that was never actually measured.

risks_and_mitigations.risk: The platform's decisive-decomposition bias is conditional on behaviour verifiability, and that precondition is unmet. risks_and_mitigations.mitigation: Make the rules reachable by extracting them into a referencable library with a public entry point, then pin today's OBSERVED behaviour with characterisation tests — including the specified-but-unimplemented 'Conjured' rule and the self-cancelling zeroing branch — BEFORE any transformation. This is a precondition, not a follow-up.

review_asks.title: What is the migration disposition for this application? A provisional value was recorded because none was supplied.
review_asks.why: The recorded disposition drives downstream sizing, sequencing and cost, and this one was derived from technical evidence rather than ruled by anyone — so an unreviewed placeholder could harden into a plan of record.
review_asks.assessment: No target plan was supplied to this analysis, so no disposition has actually been decided for this application. The output format requires one, and 'replatform' was recorded as the only option the evidence supports: the application runs on a Windows-only framework that left Microsoft support in 2016, while the target environment is a Linux container platform on a modern runtime, and there is no in-place upgrade path. Recording 'retain' would have contradicted that evidence. The decision itself belongs to the disposition line, not to this analysis.
review_asks.reasoning: Two measured facts force a platform move: the end-of-support Windows-only runtime, and an entry point that blocks waiting for a keypress, which would never terminate under a container orchestrator. Those point away from 'retain'. What the evidence cannot settle is the choice between porting a 172-line program and simply retiring or rewriting it — at this size, replacement may well cost less than a port, and that is a portfolio judgment about whether the capability is still needed at all, which no amount of code reading can answer.

confidence.rationale: High confidence that a platform move is unavoidable and that 'retain' is wrong; low confidence in 'replatform' specifically over retire-or-replace, because that turns on business need and cost rather than on code evidence.
